summary: A discussion of the Pcmail workstation-based distributed mail system, identical to RFC 993 except for a new, much simpler mail transport protocol. That change came from continued research into making protocols easier to implement and use. It replaces RFC 993.

eli5.summary: It is the same plan as an earlier memo for a shared mailbox, but with a simpler way to move the letters around.

questions: how does the pcmail transport protocol work
subtitle: A 1988 design for mail kept on a central repository, with small personal computers that sync a local copy over a simple text protocol.

tldr.problem: People owned several workstations, some tiny and some only occasionally on a network, and still wanted their mail available and consistent on all of them.
tldr.mechanism: A permanent repository stores each user's mail state, and clients keep a local copy that they synchronize using DMSP, a text request/response protocol on TCP port 158. Each message is split into a roughly 100-byte descriptor and a body, so small clients can hold summaries only.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1056 replaces RFC 993 and is identical to it in its discussion, except that it describes a new, much simpler transport protocol. It is an Informational RFC.

today: RFC 1056 is an Informational RFC that obsoletes RFC 993, and the unit metadata lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The RFC describes the system as used by a small community at MIT's Laboratory for Computer Science at the time of writing.

sections.title: Why Pcmail Exists
sections.content:
Pcmail is a distributed mail system for users who each own one or more workstations. The workstations range from resource-limited machines like the IBM PC to resource-rich machines like Suns or Microvaxes. Some are connected to a network all the time, others only now and then, and Pcmail is meant to serve all of them, including diskless workstations.

The system has two halves. A single repository is the storage center for incoming mail and keeps a stable copy of each user's mail, called the global mail state. Any number of clients, typically single-user workstations, each keep a local copy called the local mail state. Because a client may be offline, the two copies can differ, so they must be synchronized.

This RFC is a discussion of the system. It states that it is identical to the discussion in RFC 993, except that a new, much simpler mail transport protocol is described.
sections.eli5: There is one big mailbox that is always open, and each of your computers keeps its own copy. Some computers are small or are not always plugged in, so the system has to cope with that.

sections.title: The Repository and Its Objects
sections.content:
The repository should be a permanent network site with a powerful processor and lots of disk, because clients and people sending mail both rely on it being available at any time. It stores mail, talks to clients, and translates Internet mail into its own namespace.

Each user is a user object with a unique name, a password, a list of client objects, a list of subscription objects and a list of mailbox objects. A client object has a unique name and a status of active or inactive. A client that has not connected for a set period (one week in the implementation described) is inactive, and on its next connection it is told to reset itself and fetch a fresh copy of the state.

Messages live in mailboxes. Each mailbox records its total messages, its unseen messages and its next available message unique identifier (UID). Bboard mailboxes hold bulletin board mail: their names are unique across the whole repository, and subscribers get read-only access and track what they have seen with a subscription object.

Each message is split into a descriptor and a body. The descriptor holds the UID, the size in bytes and lines, the date, to, from and subject header fields, and sixteen flags numbered 0 through 15. Flags 0 to 7 are defined for repository use (deleted, seen, forwarded to the user, forwarded by the user, filed, printed, replied to, copied) and flags 8 to 15 are free for users. A message is identified by the triple of user name, mailbox name and message UID. Address objects map RFC 822 style addresses to a user and mailbox pair so incoming Internet mail reaches the right place.
sections.eli5: Every message gets a small summary card plus the full letter. The card is tiny, so even a very small computer can keep all the cards and fetch the letters when it has room.

sections.title: DMSP, the Client-Repository Protocol
sections.content:
The Distributed Mail System Protocol (DMSP) was completely re-specified in this version. It used to run on top of the USP remote-procedure-call protocol, which was not fully specified anywhere, so it was hard to implement on other systems. DMSP is now a simple request/response protocol similar to SMTP or NNTP, running directly on a reliable byte stream such as TCP. The TCP contact port is 158.

A request is an operation name followed by arguments, ended with a carriage-return and line-feed. Operation names are case-insensitive, arguments are case-insensitive but case-preserving, an argument is at most 64 characters, and a line is at most 512 characters including the line ending. Every operation gets a three-digit reply code. The first digit says what happened: 1XX informative, 2XX success, 3XX success with text to follow, 4XX failed, 5XX syntax error. Text lists end with a single period on its own line, and a data line that starts with a period has the period doubled so it cannot end the list by accident.

A session starts with login (user, password, client name, a create-client flag and a batch-mode flag) and ends with logout. All operations are failure-atomic: they either succeed completely or leave the mail state unchanged, and an operation counts as failed unless an explicit acknowledgement arrives. Operations fall into groups for general use, users, clients, mailboxes, addresses, subscriptions and messages, for example list-mailboxes, fetch-changed-descriptors, fetch-message, copy-message and set-message-flag. The send-version operation should come first, to catch version skew.

Passwords are sent in clear text, because encryption is hard on resource-poor clients. The RFC itself says this is not an acceptable long-term solution and welcomes alternatives.
sections.eli5: The client and the repository talk by typing short lines to each other, like texting. Each line gets a numbered answer, and if anything goes wrong halfway, everything is put back the way it was.

sections.title: Synchronizing Local and Global State
sections.content:
Rare changes such as adding or deleting mailboxes and addresses are synchronized by comparing lists from list-mailboxes and list-address. The common changes are to descriptors: a flag changes, a descriptor is created by new mail or a copy, or a descriptor is destroyed by expunge-mailbox.

The repository keeps an update list for each client, naming the messages that changed since that client last synchronized. The client runs fetch-changed-descriptors, giving a mailbox and a maximum count. It gets back either an expunged line plus a UID, so it removes the local message, or a six-line descriptor that it stores. Then it calls reset-descriptors with a UID range to mark the changes as recorded, so they are not sent again unless they change again.

Clients can work in two modes. In interactive mode the client is always connected and every local change is immediately sent to the repository. In batch mode the client queues local changes, then on the next connection sends them all and afterwards synchronizes. Because a descriptor is about 100 bytes regardless of message size, most clients can hold all descriptors, and a very small client can hold a subset and use fetch-message or print-message for the bodies.
sections.eli5: The big mailbox keeps a to-do list for each computer: what changed since it last checked. The computer reads the list, copies the changes into its notebook, and crosses them off.

sections.title: A Sample Session and the Implementation
sections.content:
The RFC walks through a session for a user named Fred whose client is office-client. After the banner 200 Pcmail repository version 3.0.0 ready, the client logs in, lists mailboxes, and calls fetch-changed-descriptors fred 10. The reply holds two expunged UIDs, one changed descriptor and one new descriptor. The client updates its local copy and then sends reset-descriptors fred 1 2312. When it then tries to pull a 320-line message and runs out of disk space, the atomic rule means the partial copy is thrown away and the message is simply marked off line.

The implementation described serves a small community. The repository is written in C and runs under UNIX on a DEC Microvax-II. The IBM PC clients work only in batch mode, with a mail reader written in the Epsilon editor's EEL language. The UNIX clients are fully interactive, with a mail reader inside GNU-EMACS, and a repository locking scheme stops one client modifying state while another is doing so. The RFC reports that the system is used by a small community at the MIT Laboratory for Computer Science and performs well with up to ten users connected.
sections.eli5: In the example, Fred's computer reads the to-do list, updates its notebook, and then tries to copy one huge letter. It runs out of room, so it throws away the half copy and just remembers that the letter is waiting.
